wiki/Act_of_Congress#Public_law,_private_law,_designation "Act of Congress") [95–511](https://uslaw.link/citation/us-law/public/95/511), 92 [Stat.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Statutes_at_Large "United States Statutes at Large") [1783](https://legislink.org/us/stat-92-1783), [50 U.S.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_50_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 50 of the United States Code") [ch. 36](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/50/chapter-36)) is a [United States federal law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_United_States "Law of the United States") that establishes procedures for the [surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance "Surveillance") and collection of foreign intelligence on domestic soil.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

FISA was enacted in response to revelations of widespread privacy violations by the federal government [under President Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Richard_Nixon "Presidency of Richard Nixon"). It requires [federal law enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_law_enforcement_in_the_United_States "Federal law enforcement in the United States") and [intelligence agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Intelligence_Community "United States Intelligence Community") to obtain authorization for gathering "foreign intelligence information" between "foreign powers" and "agents of foreign powers" suspected of [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage "Espionage") or [terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism "Terrorism").[[2]](#cite_note-fisa-2) The law established the [Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Court "Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court") (FISC) to oversee requests for surveillance warrants.

Although FISA was initially limited to government use of electronic surveillance, subsequent amendments have broadened the law to regulate other intelligence-gathering methods, including physical searches, [pen register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen_register "Pen register") and [trap and trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_and_trace_device "Trap and trace device") (PR/TT) devices, and compelling the production of certain types of business records.[[3]](#cite_note-:702-3)

FISA has been repeatedly amended since the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"), with several added provisions garnering political and public controversy due to privacy concerns.[[4]](#cite_note-Sabin-4)

## History and background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Act&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and background")]

The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) was introduced on May 18, 1977, by Senator [Ted Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy") and was signed into law by President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") on 25 October 1978. The bill was cosponsored by nine senators: [Birch Bayh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_Bayh "Birch Bayh"), [James O. Eastland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_O._Eastland "James O. Eastland"), [Jake Garn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_Garn "Jake Garn"), [Walter Huddleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Huddleston "Walter Huddleston"), [Daniel Inouye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Inouye "Daniel Inouye"), [Charles Mathias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mathias "Charles Mathias"), [John L. McClellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_L._McClellan "John L. McClellan"), [Gaylord Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaylord_Nelson "Gaylord Nelson"), and [Strom Thurmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strom_Thurmond "Strom Thurmond").

The FISA resulted from extensive investigations by [Senate Committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate#Committees "United States Senate") into the legality of domestic [intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_(information_gathering) "Intelligence (information gathering)") activities. These investigations were led separately by [Sam Ervin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Ervin "Sam Ervin") and [Frank Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Church "Frank Church") in 1978 as a response to President [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon")'s usage of federal resources, including law enforcement agencies, to spy on political and activist groups.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-Arrigo2014-6) The law itself was crafted in large part in closed door meetings between legislators and members of the [Justice Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice").[[7]](#cite_note-Gottfried2003-7)

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 3B.5 Research Note

**Lens:** 3B.5 — Did the ruler use emergency powers, security laws, surveillance, anti-terror measures, or administrative controls narrowly and lawfully, or as tools for intimidation, collective punishment, and control?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mixed**, characterized by **broad continuation of inherited security-law frameworks** without major expansion, but with **selective use of administrative controls** that raised concerns. The strongest favorable 2023 actions include the **AI Executive Order's civil-rights safeguards** (Oct 30, 2023), the **National Cybersecurity Strategy's defender-focused approach** (March 2023), the **continuation of FISA Section 702** with reforms, and the **administration's refusal to use military force domestically** against protesters. The strongest negative 2023 actions include the **continued Title 42 expulsion framework** (until May 11, 2023), the **Gaza war selective narrative framing**, and the **expanded use of sanctions and export controls**. The administration generally did not use emergency powers for political intimidation but did use administrative controls extensively for immigration and sanctions. Net assessment: **mixed but restrained**, with structural concerns about administrative-control expansion.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — FISA Section 702 reauthorization in 2024 (post-2023)

- **Title / source:** Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects FISA Section 702 history through 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Act
- **Summary:** The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (FISA) establishes procedures for surveillance and collection of foreign intelligence on domestic soil. Section 702 of FISA was due to expire at the end of 2023 and was reauthorized by Congress in April 2024 with significant reforms. The Biden administration supported the Section 702 reauthorization with reforms including new court oversight of FBI queries and minimization procedures. In 2023, Biden did not expand FISA authority beyond existing scope.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (mixed — continued surveillance framework but with reforms)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 2 — AI Executive Order (Oct 30, 2023) civil-rights safeguards

- **Title / source:** Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia / The White House
- **Date:** October 30, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- **Summary:** The AI Executive Order 14110 included explicit civil-rights safeguards, requiring the Department of Justice to coordinate civil-rights enforcement of AI systems. The EO ordered agencies to address AI-related civil-rights harms, including discrimination in housing, employment, and law enforcement. The civil-rights safeguards represented use of administrative authority to protect rather than suppress rights.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — administrative authority used to protect civil rights)
- **Also informs:** 1B.9, 3B.1, 7B.6

### Claim 3 — Title 42 expired May 11, 2023; transition to Title 8

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** May 11, 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Biden administration allowed Title 42 — the COVID-19-era public health expulsion authority — to expire on May 11, 2023. After expiration, immigration enforcement returned to standard Title 8 authorities. The Biden administration implemented new parole programs (e.g., CHNV parole for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, Venezuelans) and rule-making to manage post-Title-42 migration flows. The decision to allow Title 42 to expire was a return to standard immigration law, ending the emergency public-health authority.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — expiration of emergency power)
- **Also informs:** 2B.5, 3B.2

### Claim 4 — No 2023 use of National Guard against domestic protesters

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking National Guard deployment or military force against domestic protesters. The Trump-era precedent of military deployment against Lafayette Square protesters (June 2020) was not repeated in 2023. The administration's approach to protest was through civilian law enforcement.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — no military use against protesters)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 3B.2, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 5 — Continued sanctions enforcement: OFAC, BIS

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Biden administration continued sanctions enforcement via Treasury OFAC and Commerce BIS throughout 2023, targeting Russian entities involved in Iranian missile and drone supply chains, Iranian nuclear-related entities, North Korean entities, and others. The sanctions represent administrative controls used for foreign-policy purposes. The scale of sanctions enforcement expanded in 2023 with new designations related to the Russia-Ukraine war and other geopolitical events.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working against 3B.5 — expanded sanctions use of administrative controls)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 6 — AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023) administrative-control precedent

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 San Diego announcement
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** The AUKUS submarine deal required the AUKUS Submarine Authorization Act and a bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement that lowered the bar for non-proliferation precedent. The administrative-control precedent allowed nuclear-propulsion technology transfer to a non-NPT state. The deal required extensive administrative coordination across U.S. agencies.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working against 3B.5 — administrative-control precedent for nonproliferation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.6, 2B.2

### Claim 7 — AI Safety and Security Board (per EO 14110)

- **Title / source:** Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Established by EO 14110 (Oct 30, 2023); membership named in early 2024
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- **Summary:** The AI EO established the AI Safety and Security Board under DHS to coordinate AI safety efforts across critical-infrastructure sectors. The Board represented administrative structure for managing AI risks, including CBRN risks from frontier AI models.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — administrative structure for risk management)
- **Also informs:** 1B.9, 3B.4

### Claim 8 — Public attribution of cyber-espionage campaigns in 2023

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Biden administration continued to publicly attribute major cyber-espionage campaigns in 2023, including the Microsoft Exchange Online compromise (Chinese state-sponsored actor Storm-0558), MOVEit file-transfer data breach (Russian-speaking CL0P ransomware gang), and ongoing Iranian cyber activity. The public attribution represents use of intelligence-community capabilities for transparency rather than suppression.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — public attribution of cyber-espionage)
- **Also informs:** 1B.9, 3B.4

### Claim 9 — National Cybersecurity Strategy (March 2023) defensive framing

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** March 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** The March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy rebalanced responsibility toward "defenders" (and away from end-users) and signaled regulatory baselines for critical-infrastructure operators (including nuclear and energy sectors). The strategy rebalanced the burden of cybersecurity defense toward those most able to bear it, rather than using surveillance or anti-terror measures to monitor end-users. The framework is administrative authority used defensively rather than for control.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — administrative authority used defensively)
- **Also informs:** 1B.9, 3B.4

### Claim 10 — No 2023 invocation of Insurrection Act or martial law

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking the Insurrection Act, declaring martial law, or using military force for domestic political purposes. The administration did not expand the post-9/11 emergency powers framework beyond existing scope.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — no expansion of emergency powers)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 11 — Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023): coalition maritime-security operation

- **Title / source:** Red Sea crisis
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Crisis began Oct 19, 2023; Operation Prosperity Guardian launched Dec 18, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis
- **Summary:** Operation Prosperity Guardian was a U.S.-led multinational coalition (12+ countries) operating under coalition command in the Red Sea to defend freedom of navigation against Houthi attacks. The operation used military capability for a defensive coalition mission, with allied consent and international legal authority (right of self-defense under UN Charter Art. 51).
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — defensive coalition operation)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.4, 8B.4

### Claim 12 — Libya/Tunisia/Sudan non-intervention in 2023

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, the Biden administration did not deploy U.S. forces for direct intervention in Libya, Tunisia, or Sudan. The administration's response to the Sudanese civil war (Apr 15, 2023 onward) was diplomatic through special envoy Mike Hammer, sanctions on RSF, and evacuation coordination. The restraint avoided the use of force for regime-change purposes.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.5 (working for 3B.5 — restraint from direct intervention)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.7, 7B.6, 8B.4

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 3B.5

- **Continued sanctions enforcement expansion** — administrative-control expansion.
- **AUKUS precedent** — administrative-control precedent for nonproliferation.
- **Selective narrative framing on Gaza war** — narrative as administrative control.
- **Title 42 use until May 2023** — emergency-power continuation.

## Favorable evidence on 3B.5

- **FISA Section 702 reauthorization with reforms** — surveillance with accountability.
- **AI EO civil-rights safeguards** — administrative authority used to protect.
- **Title 42 expired May 11, 2023** — emergency-power expiration.
- **No 2023 National Guard use against protesters** — no domestic military use.
- **Public attribution of cyber-espionage** — public transparency.
- **National Cybersecurity Strategy defensive** — administrative authority defensively.
- **No 2023 Insurrection Act or martial law** — no emergency-power expansion.
- **Operation Prosperity Guardian coalition** — defensive coalition.
- **Libya/Tunisia/Sudan non-intervention** — restraint from intervention.
- **Hur investigation cooperation** — accountability-process cooperation.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 OFAC sanctions designations** — public but not detailed.
  - **The 2023 CISA cybersecurity advisories and BODs** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 emergency-power declarations** — public but not detailed.
  - **The 2023 National Security Memorandum on AI** — finalized in 2024.
  - **The 2023 DHS parole programs detail** — public but not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 ICE detention statistics** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 FBI surveillance statistics** — public but not detailed.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 OFAC sanctions designations list, (b) the 2023 CISA cybersecurity advisories, (c) the 2023 emergency-power declarations, (d) the 2024 National Security Memorandum on AI, (e) the 2023 DHS parole programs detail, (f) the 2023 ICE detention data, and (g) the 2023 FBI surveillance statistics.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 3B.5 is the **continued use of administrative controls without major expansion of emergency powers**. The strongest favorable items are Title 42 expiration, no Insurrection Act, public cyber attribution, and no National Guard against protesters. The strongest unfavorable items are sanctions enforcement expansion and AUKUS precedent.
